extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, and advanced law students (UK patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for determining infringement, defenses, remedies, and interlocutory practice in patent actions (principally UK cases and statutes). Covers what constitutes infringement by manufacture, sale, user, importation, possession, and when courts will grant interlocutory relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of material claims and chemical equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention claimed is for the use of a particular metallic substance (e.g. carburet of manganese in definite proportions), the use of different substances (e.g. coal-tar and oxide of manganese) will not infringe unless such substances were known equivalents at the date of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court considered whether at the date of the patent persons acquainted with the subject knew coal-tar and oxide of manganese would be chemical equivalents; a discovery made after the patent date may itself be the subject of a new patent. If the specification truly limits the invention to a particular substance and no equivalent was known at the date, there is no evidence of infringement (cases: Heath et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition proportions and claim breadth for alloys
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inventor states the most suitable proportions of ingredients for a composition (e.g. an alloy), another person will not be allowed to evade the patent by employing somewhat different proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to compositions that specify particular proportions will be construed to cover those proportions and closely similar ones if the inventor has stated them as the suitable proportions known to him (case: Muntz v. Foster and Collins). Evidence about purity of metals and practicability of following earlier directions is relevant to distinguishing prior compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements by equivalent operations known at patent date
rubrics_metrics.description: If improvements on a patented chemical process produce the same result by operations that were known to be equivalent at the date of the patent, implementing them will constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the defendant's processes are praiseworthy and produce the result differently, if they employ the same materials and produce exactly the same result using equivalent operations known at the patent date, they are not a different invention (case: Badische Anilin und Soda Fabrik v. Levinstein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing in articles made in infringement (sale/import) is infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale by a dealer of articles made in infringement of a patent is itself an infringement, and it is not necessary for the patentee to prove that the dealer was aware they were made surreptitiously by a patented process; this applies equally to articles made abroad and imported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities include Wright v. Hitchcock; Davenport v. Hylands; Walton v. Larter; Von Heyden v. Neustadt. Importation by licensees under foreign patents does not avoid liability under the British patent in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of sale is prima facie evidence of infringement (but exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the plaintiff gives prima facie evidence of infringement by proving the patented article was sold by the defendant, he is not ordinarily bound to prove that the article was not obtained from himself, his licensees, or persons to whom he had sold it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstances may require the patentee to prove not only the sale but that the article was not made and sold by himself or his agents (e.g. Betts v. Willmott). The specifics of distribution and manufacture may shift evidential burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to prove manufacture by patented method for process patents
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patent is for a method of manufacture, production of an article similar to the plaintiff's is not, without more, evidence that it was made by the patented method; the manner of manufacture must be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In process patents the plaintiff should show how the defendant's article was produced because the same result may be obtainable by a different (non-infringing) method (cases: Palmar v. Jennison). However, production of articles with the essential qualities and possession of necessary machines may suffice in some cases (Jastrzebski v. ???; Hall v. Boot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of articles with essential qualities may be prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The production (and sale) of pieces of an article having the essential qualities of the patented article can be prima facie evidence of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Jastrzebski (pieces of rope) and Hall v. Boot indicate that where the defendant's product manifests the essential qualities of the patented article—and relevant machinery is present—this can support an inference of infringement absent explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making/stockpiling may amount to infringement even without sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacture or production of infringing articles (e.g. making ten tons of metal sheathing) may be an infringement even where no sale is proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that large scale manufacture demonstrates infringing activity (e.g. Muntz v. Foster), and mere exposure/offer for sale may in some cases amount to infringement (contrasting case law exists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by user (including use of imported articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may recover from users of infringing articles; use in the UK of articles made abroad that are subject to a British patent is illegal even when the user is passive (e.g. in transit), depending on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Betts v. Neilson and subsequent authorities show that transshipment or use in the UK can be held a user of the invention when the patented feature is necessary for the article (bottles with capsules for beer). However, there may be hypothetical cases (tools packed inert for transit) where no user is found. Context and the nature of the use (active vs passive) matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession indicating intended use can justify injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of articles made in infringement may be enough to obtain an injunction without proving active user if circumstances show intended use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: injunction against a shipmaster restraining him from using pumps placed on board; although actual user was not proved, the master acted with makers asserting right to use the pumps (case: Man v. ? / United Telephone v. ?). Courts look to conduct showing intention to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicarious liability: employer and agent both liable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where infringement is committed through an agent, both employer and agent are liable; the agent cannot justify by saying he acted under orders of the principal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Gibson v. Brand; Betts v. De Vitre; Sykes v. Howarth; Spencer v. Ancoats Vale Rubber Co. Liability extends to acts done by servants or agents in the course of their employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim injunctions against carriers and restraining import/export
rubrics_metrics.description: Steamship carriers may be restrained by interim injunction from importing or exporting goods alleged to have been made in infringement and from parting with possession when the validity of the patent has been proved in action against another person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases include Washburn Co. v. Canard Co.; courts will restrain carriers once validity is established elsewhere and appropriate circumstances exist, even if goods were manufactured abroad and no on-board user occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign vessels exemption under Patents Act s.43 (1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an invention for navigation of a foreign vessel within UK jurisdiction, or use in a foreign vessel within that jurisdiction, is not deemed infringement unless used for manufacture or preparation of something intended for sale in or export from the UK/Isle of Man; exceptions apply where foreign state doesn't reciprocate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 43(1)-(2) of the Patents Act 1883 governs this. Cases falling outside s.43 are governed by earlier common law decisions (e.g. Cailnill v. Van Vlissingen). Reciprocity exceptions for foreign states apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crown use and patents (pre- and post-Patents Act 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically grants by the Crown were construed to permit Crown use without royalties; by s.27 of the Patents Act 1883 patents granted on applications after the Act have like effect against the Crown as against subjects, but Crown departments may use an invention for public service with Treasury-approved terms or terms settled by the Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feather v. The Queen established pre-1883 Crown privileges. Dixon v. The London Small Arms Company limited contractors' Crown privilege when they were not servants/agents of the Crown. Treasury approval/terms apply for Crown use under the 1883 Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different means to achieve same result is not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patentee is limited to the particular combination described in his specification, another person may lawfully effect the same object by employing different means; mere attainment of the same end is not infringement if means differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases illustrate that substituting different structural or procedural means (even producing the same outcome) can avoid infringement if the patented combination is not used (examples: submarine cable apparatus cases). The limitations of the specification determine scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-infringement for making as model or bona fide experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing a patented machine as an amusement or model, or making the patented article for bona fide experiment and not for commercial profit, is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jones v. Pearce; Frearson v. Loe. Example: using a patented sewage-precipitating process solely to purify sewage without deriving profit from the product was held not infringing (Higgs/Goodwin example). The purpose and profit motive are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a part to a different purpose may not infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of a new and material part of an arrangement to a purpose different from that to which it is applied in the patented combination does not necessarily infringe the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that changing the purpose or context of an element may avoid infringement; look to authorities cited on application-to-purpose distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of a specification alone is not infringement; use is required
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere publication of a specification is not an infringement of a prior patent; it is the use of the earlier invention that constitutes infringement. The defendant's specification is of little importance on the question of infringement compared with actual use or manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per L. J. Brett in Otis v. Linford: no infringement until the patented mode is worked or made by another. The question of practical use controls infringement inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural substance exception and revival by patented process
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a natural mineral substance to effect a purpose is not an infringement of a patent obtained for applying an artificial substance of the same chemical constitution, unless the natural substance has been revivified or treated by the patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: patent for purifying coal gas by hydrated oxide of iron (artificial) — using natural bog ochre containing oxide of iron was held not infringing; but use after revivification by the patented process could be restrained (case: Hills v. Liverpool Gas Light Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplying materials and indemnities: limited supplier liability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an infringement to sell chemical substances knowing the buyer intends to use them in infringing the patent; nor is it an infringement to indemnify the buyer if the patent is disputed or likely to be so. However, if buyer and seller know the patent to be valid, an indemnity agreement may be void against public policy, and the seller would not thereby be guilty of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases and commentary (Townsend v. Haworth; Sykes v. Howarth) show nuanced law on supplier liability: knowledge of intent alone does not automatically make a supplier liable as an infringer; the validity of the patent and public policy on indemnities affect enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts on board British vessels at Malta or on high seas not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for the United Kingdom will not be infringed by acts done on board a British vessel at Malta or on the high seas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newatt v. Elliott: territoriality of patent rights matters; acts outside UK jurisdiction are generally not infringements of UK patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by foreign sovereigns and limits of court jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a foreign sovereign legally owns articles made in infringement of a British patent and brings them into England to place on a warship, the courts may lack jurisdiction to prevent removal of such articles due to sovereign immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Vavasseur v. Krupp; practical limit to injunctive relief against foreign sovereigns or their property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention of infringer is immaterial to liability
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining infringement, the intention of the alleged infringer is immaterial; an innocent or ignorant party who violates the patentee's rights is still liable to compensate for the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (Stead v. Anderson; statements from Shumaker v. ?, Heath v. Pierin etc.) emphasize that the action is maintainable in respect of what the defendant does, not what he intends. Courts may, however, exercise equitable discretion in relief (see innocent/trivial infringement entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable discretion for innocent, trivial, or negligible infringements and delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Where infringement is innocent, accidental, trivial, and not substantially damaging, or where the patentee has been negligent or delayed in prosecuting rights, courts may refuse injunctions or exercise discretion in relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Betts v. Willmott (retail dealer sold in ignorance; injunction dismissed). Delay or negligence by the patentee can defeat interlocutory relief; explained delay may be excused (United Telegraph Co. examples). Courts weigh conduct, prejudice, and need for final trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunction principles in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts grant interlocutory (interim) injunctions when the patentee can make out a proper case — typically when the patent is old and has been enjoyed undisturbed, when validity has been established elsewhere, or when defendant's conduct makes validity uncontested; where the patent is of recent date and validity is disputed the Court will generally refuse injunction and send the patentee to establish validity at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Eldon's principle: the Court will not act on presumed validity where specification defects or validity are contested without prior legal trial. Court will grant interim relief for long possession, multiple favorable suits, or established validity in another jurisdiction. Requirements include showing actual public user (in some cases), absence of negligence/delay by patentee, and that infringement is not a matter of serious doubt. If infringement is doubtful, injunction will be refused until trial; if there is reason to suppose a new trial will be obtained, relief may be withheld. Cases: Hill v. Thompson; Dudgeon v. Thomson; Losh v. Hague; Muntz v. Foster; Renard v. Levinstein; Collard v. Allison; others collected in the chapter.
